item.title: Cost of rental voids up 58% in three years
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The financial impact of rental void periods has increased dramatically across the UK private rental sector, with landlords facing significantly longer periods of empty properties and lost income. Recent analysis reveals the average cost of rental voids has surged by 58% over the past three years, creating substantial pressure for property investors.

Understanding the growing void period challenge

Void periods – the time between tenancies when a rental property sits empty – have become notably more expensive for landlords. Several factors contribute to this trend, including:

  • Longer average void durations compared to pre-pandemic levels
  • Higher mortgage interest rates increasing holding costs
  • Rising property maintenance expenses during vacant periods
  • Increased local authority licensing requirements in some areas

Industry experts suggest that void periods which previously lasted weeks may now extend to several months in certain regions, particularly where rental demand has softened or where landlords need to undertake significant property upgrades between tenancies.

Strategies to mitigate void period costs

While void periods are an inevitable part of property investment, landlords might consider several approaches to minimise their financial impact:

  • Market research: Keeping rental prices competitive through regular local market reviews could help attract tenants more quickly
  • Property presentation: Investing in professional photography and staging may make properties more appealing to prospective renters
  • Flexible tenancies: Offering different contract lengths might appeal to a broader range of tenants
  • Pre-emptive maintenance: Addressing repair issues during tenancies could reduce turnaround time between lets

Some landlords are exploring alternative rental models such as corporate lets or short-term holiday rentals (subject to local regulations) to reduce void periods, though these approaches come with their own considerations and potential risks.

As the private rental sector continues to evolve, landlords may need to adapt their strategies to manage the growing financial impact of void periods. Keeping abreast of local market conditions and maintaining properties to a high standard could prove crucial in navigating this challenging environment.

item.title: Inheritance boom could bring thousands more landlords
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A surge in inheritances across the UK could lead to a significant rise in the number of landlords, as intergenerational wealth transfers open doors to property investment opportunities. With younger generations increasingly benefiting from inherited assets, many may consider entering the buy-to-let market to grow their wealth further.

The Impact of Rising Inheritances

Recent trends indicate that wealth transfers from older to younger generations are on the rise. As baby boomers pass on their assets, a growing number of individuals are finding themselves in a position to invest in property. For some, this could mean purchasing additional homes to let, potentially boosting the private rental sector.

Whilst inheritances provide a financial springboard, becoming a landlord requires careful consideration. Prospective investors might weigh up factors such as mortgage options, rental yields, and the responsibilities of managing a property. Additionally, changes in tax regulations and evolving tenant rights could influence decisions in this area.

Opportunities and Challenges in Buy-to-Let

For those considering entering the buy-to-let market, there are both opportunities and challenges to navigate. On one hand, rising property prices in certain regions could offer long-term capital growth, whilst rental demand remains strong in many areas. On the other hand, increased regulation and higher costs, such as stamp duty and maintenance expenses, may pose hurdles for new landlords.

Borrowers might explore specialist buy-to-let mortgages, which are tailored to property investors. These products often require larger deposits and come with different eligibility criteria compared to residential mortgages. Seeking professional financial advice could help individuals make informed decisions about whether buy-to-let is the right path for them.

As the property market continues to evolve, inheritances could play a pivotal role in shaping its future. For those with newfound wealth, investing in property may be an appealing option, but thorough research and planning remain essential to success.

item.title: Holiday let profit lost if reclassification goes ahead – claim
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Proposed tax changes for holiday lets could significantly reduce profitability for property investors and impact local economies in tourism-reliant areas, according to recent analysis. The potential reclassification of short-term rental properties may alter the financial landscape for those operating in this sector.

Potential impact on holiday let returns

Industry experts suggest that the planned tax adjustments might substantially decrease net yields for holiday let owners. Current projections indicate that some operators could see their profits diminish by nearly a quarter if the reforms proceed as outlined. The changes primarily concern how properties are categorised for tax purposes, potentially shifting many holiday lets into a higher taxation bracket.

These adjustments come as the government examines ways to balance the holiday let market with the need for residential housing in popular tourist destinations. However, critics argue the measures may inadvertently harm smaller operators whilst failing to address underlying housing shortages.

Concerns for tourism-dependent communities

Local economies in coastal towns and rural hotspots may face particular challenges if the tax changes discourage holiday let investments. Many businesses in these areas – from cafes to activity providers – rely heavily on visitors staying in short-term rentals. A reduction in available holiday accommodation could lead to fewer tourists and lower spending in these regions.

Industry bodies have highlighted that the proposed reforms might disproportionately affect certain areas. Cornwall, the Lake District and other popular staycation destinations could see significant economic repercussions if property owners reconsider their investment strategies due to reduced profitability.

Considering alternative property strategies

Property investors concerned about the potential changes might explore diversifying their portfolios. Some options could include shifting focus to traditional buy-to-let properties, exploring commercial hospitality investments, or considering properties in areas less likely to be affected by tourism taxes.

Those currently operating holiday lets may wish to review their financial projections and consult professional advisers to understand how the proposed changes could affect their specific circumstances. Many experts recommend staying informed about the consultation process, as the final details of any reforms may differ from initial proposals.

While the government's intention appears to be creating a fairer property market, the balance between regulating the sector and supporting local tourism economies remains a complex challenge. The consultation period may provide opportunities for stakeholders to share their perspectives before any final decisions are made.

item.title: September house price growth halves
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK housing market has shown signs of slowing down, with Nationwide’s latest report revealing that house price growth halved in September. Rising mortgage costs appear to be a key factor influencing buyer demand and market activity, creating a more subdued environment for property values.

Understanding the slowdown

According to Nationwide’s data, the pace of house price growth has significantly decreased, with September’s figures showing a marked reduction compared to previous months. This slowdown suggests that affordability pressures, particularly driven by higher mortgage rates, are beginning to weigh on potential buyers. Many homeowners and prospective purchasers might be reconsidering their plans amidst these financial challenges.

Additionally, the broader economic climate, including inflation and rising living costs, could be contributing to this trend. With household budgets under strain, the ability to save for deposits or afford higher monthly mortgage payments has become more difficult for some buyers.

The impact of rising mortgage costs

Mortgage rates have been climbing steadily, influenced by the Bank of England’s base rate increases. This has led to higher borrowing costs for those looking to secure new mortgages or remortgage existing ones. For first-time buyers, in particular, these rising costs could be a significant barrier to entering the property market.

Existing homeowners may also face challenges if they are nearing the end of fixed-rate mortgage deals. With remortgaging potentially leading to higher monthly payments, some borrowers might find themselves needing to reassess their financial plans. Seeking independent financial advice could be a prudent step for those navigating these changes.

What does this mean for the housing market?

While the slowdown in house price growth may offer some relief to buyers who have been struggling with affordability, it also highlights the complexities of the current market. Sellers might need to adjust their expectations, recognising that the rapid price increases seen in recent years may not be sustainable in the current climate.

For those considering entering the market, it could be worth exploring fixed-rate mortgage options to lock in current rates and provide stability against potential future increases. Additionally, staying informed about market trends and seeking professional guidance may help borrowers make more informed decisions.

As the UK housing market continues to evolve, keeping a close eye on economic developments and mortgage rate changes will be crucial for both buyers and sellers. While the current slowdown presents challenges, it also offers opportunities for those who are prepared to navigate this shifting landscape.

item.title: Jobs at risk as property giant announces major shake-up
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property consultancy giant JLL has announced plans to close its UK planning division, potentially affecting at least 25 employees across five offices. The restructuring could lead to redundancies in London, Bristol, Manchester, Leeds and Edinburgh as the firm reassesses its business priorities.

Restructuring follows leadership changes

The proposed closure comes after several senior management shifts at JLL. In April 2025, Matt Richards took over as UK chief executive, replacing Stephanie Hyde. This followed his previous role leading capital markets across Europe, the Middle East and Africa. The planning division currently operates under Raoul Veevers, who joined from Cluttons in 2022, and regional lead Joanna Gabrilatsou, a JLL veteran since 2011.

This isn't the first round of job cuts at the consultancy. Just one month after Richards' appointment, JLL eliminated nearly 150 positions within its UK property and asset management operations. The company hasn't disclosed the final number of redundancies expected from this latest restructuring.

Strategic review prompts difficult decisions

In an official statement, JLL explained: "We continually evaluate our business to align services with strategic priorities and client requirements. This has led to the challenging but necessary proposal that some roles may become redundant." The firm emphasised its confidence in existing leadership teams to maintain client service standards during the transition.

The planning division closure forms part of a broader operational review as JLL adapts to changing market conditions. Property professionals affected by the restructuring may wish to explore their options in a sector where demand for planning expertise remains steady, particularly for large-scale development projects.

Homeowners following this development might note that such corporate restructurings can sometimes signal shifting priorities in the property sector. While JLL maintains its commitment to client service, the changes reflect the ongoing evolution of consultancy services in response to economic pressures and changing client demands.

item.title: Landlord loses HMO licence after ignoring letting agent’s fire safety warnings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A Glasgow landlord has been stripped of their House in Multiple Occupation (HMO) licence after failing to address critical fire safety issues, despite warnings from their letting agent. Glasgow City Council’s licensing committee refused to renew Anna McMullan’s licence for a property on Sauchiehall Street following inspections that revealed multiple safety breaches.

Serious Safety Concerns Identified

The property, which housed five tenants, was inspected by both the council’s HMO team and the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service earlier this year. The inspections uncovered numerous hazards, including fire doors that did not close properly, blocked escape routes, and excessive combustible materials stored in utility and shower rooms. Inspectors also noted the absence of fire safety information for tenants, an incomplete electrical installation condition report, and structural issues such as holes in walls and ceilings.

The letting agent informed the committee that they had provided the landlord with several quotes for remedial work, but these were rejected. Despite repeated warnings, the landlord allegedly failed to make the necessary repairs, leaving tenants in a potentially dangerous environment.

Unresolved Issues Lead to Licence Refusal

A follow-up inspection in September revealed that many of the identified issues remained unresolved. Dust and grease had built up on extraction fans, fire doors still did not close correctly, and excessive gaps were found beneath doors. Although contractors had visited the property to quote for repairs, the work had not been completed.

Committee chairman Alex Wilson expressed concern over the lettings agent’s decision to allow new tenants to move into the property in August, despite the outstanding safety concerns. “You’ve put tenants into a property that’s not safe,” he stated, adding that the February inspection had highlighted “a huge number of deficiencies” which should have been rectified.

Lessons for Landlords and Agents

This case underscores the importance of addressing fire safety issues promptly and thoroughly. Landlords and letting agents must ensure that properties comply with safety regulations to protect tenants and maintain HMO licences. Regular inspections and timely repairs are crucial to avoid similar outcomes.

The letting agent involved has since increased the frequency of its HMO inspections, reflecting a commitment to improved safety standards. However, this incident serves as a stark reminder of the consequences of neglecting essential maintenance and compliance.

For landlords and property managers, prioritising tenant safety and adhering to regulatory requirements is not only a legal obligation but also a moral one. Failure to do so can result in severe repercussions, including the loss of licences and potential legal action.

item.title: Prime London house prices rise for first time in four years as rents accelerate
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Prime central London property prices have shown their first quarterly rise since 2020, according to fresh market data, though economic headwinds continue to cloud the recovery. Knight Frank's latest analysis reveals a 0.3% price increase between July and September, marking a tentative turnaround after four years of declines.

Market Shows Fragile Recovery Signs

The capital's prime property sector appears to be stabilising after facing multiple challenges, including mortgage rate fluctuations, tax reforms and political uncertainty. Whilst annual values remain 2% lower than September 2022, this represents the mildest year-on-year decline witnessed in the past eighteen months. Prime outer London locations have demonstrated greater resilience, with prices dipping just 0.6% over the last twelve months.

Transaction volumes provide further evidence of gradual improvement. The annual decrease in property exchanges across prime London neighbourhoods has slowed to 2.5% - a significant improvement from the 14% annual decline recorded six months earlier. The super-prime market (properties over £10 million) has also stabilised, with transaction numbers holding steady at 121 annually whilst total spending increased by 14% to £2.4 billion.

Shifting Attitudes Among Buyers and Sellers

Market participants appear to be adapting to the new financial landscape. Liza-Jane Kelly of Knight Frank observes that after years of price adjustments, sellers are demonstrating more realistic expectations: "Some properties have been listed for several years, and owners are now prioritising moving forward over holding out for peak prices."

Purchasers, meanwhile, are recognising potential value after significant price corrections. Average values in prime central London remain 22% below their 2015 highs, creating opportunities for buyers who had previously chosen to rent. Kelly notes: "When negative headlines subside, we see how quickly underlying demand resurfaces in this market."

Challenges Remain for London's Prime Market

The abolition of non-dom status earlier this year continues to impact the highest-value segments, whilst the approaching Autumn Budget introduces fresh uncertainty regarding potential property tax changes. These factors, combined with broader economic concerns, suggest the recovery may prove gradual rather than rapid.

For those considering prime London property, the current climate highlights the importance of thorough research and professional advice. Mortgage borrowers might find value in comparing products tailored for high-value purchases, whilst both buyers and sellers may wish to stay informed about potential tax developments that could affect their financial planning.

item.title: Preparing your rental property for winter weather
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

As temperatures begin to drop across the UK, landlords may wish to turn their attention to winter-proofing their rental properties. With the government investing £1.4 billion in flood defences across England for 2026/27, and meteorologists predicting potential extreme weather patterns later this year, preventative maintenance could prove particularly valuable this winter season.

Assessing flood risks and emergency planning

Property owners might consider checking whether their rental falls within a flood risk area. The government's online flood risk service allows searches by postcode, providing valuable insight into potential hazards. For properties in higher-risk locations, compiling an information pack for tenants could be beneficial, including:

  • Local emergency contact numbers
  • Details of community flood action groups
  • Instructions for reporting flooding incidents
  • Links to the government's Personal Flood Plan

Local authority websites often contain specific flood preparedness information, including locations of community hubs and details of flood wardens. Sharing these resources with tenants may help ensure they're prepared should adverse weather strike.

Conducting thorough property inspections

Before winter sets in, landlords might schedule a detailed inspection of their rental property, providing tenants with the required 24-hour notice. Key areas to examine include:

  • Gutters and drainage: Clearing blocked gutters and downpipes can prevent water damage during heavy rainfall
  • Roof condition: Checking for slipped tiles or damaged flashing could prevent leaks during storms
  • Structural integrity: Cracks in pointing or external walls may warrant attention before winter weather exacerbates damage
  • External hazards: Loose fittings, unstable fences or overhanging branches might become dangerous in high winds

Heating systems also deserve particular attention during winter inspections. Landlords may wish to verify that systems are functioning correctly, that tenants understand how to operate them efficiently, and that exposed pipes have adequate insulation. Confirming the location of the stopcock and ensuring empty properties have appropriate frost protection measures could prevent costly winter emergencies.

Whilst the UK's weather remains unpredictable, taking proactive steps to prepare rental properties for winter conditions might help landlords avoid costly repairs and ensure tenant safety throughout the colder months. Regular maintenance not only protects the property investment but also contributes to positive landlord-tenant relationships during potentially challenging weather conditions.

item.title: Estate agency expands lettings portfolio with acquisition of rival firm
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:

Kent-based Guildcrest Estates has expanded its lettings portfolio through the acquisition of fellow independent agency Frederick & Co Property Services. The enlarged portfolio will be managed by Guildcrest's existing lettings team, supported by the agency's established property management systems. While financial details remain undisclosed, the deal strengthens Guildcrest Group's position as a comprehensive property services provider across East Kent.

For landlords and tenants in the region, the merger may bring access to broader resources while maintaining the personal service associated with independent agencies. Such consolidation in the lettings market could become more common as agencies seek to enhance their service offerings and geographical coverage.

item.title: New estate agency launches for ‘standout’ homes
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The London property market has welcomed a new estate agency with a unique focus on distinctive and design-led homes. Orato Estates aims to cater to vendors whose properties stand out from the crowd, offering something beyond the standard listing. Specialising in restored period properties, architecturally unusual houses, and bespoke apartments, the agency is carving out a niche in a competitive market.

A Focus on Quality Over Quantity

Unlike traditional estate agencies that often prioritise high-volume listings, Orato Estates is taking a more selective approach. The agency plans to curate a smaller portfolio of homes that showcase exceptional architecture, interiors, and individual character. This strategy reflects its philosophy that "some homes are special because someone has put love into them." Andreas Abasaid, the agency’s founder, brings a wealth of experience from luxury marketing, creative industries, and entrepreneurship, shaping Orato’s unique vision.

item.title: London house prices could fall by £100,000 under Cleverly’s mayoral plans
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

London house prices could see a significant reduction under proposals put forward by Sir James Cleverly, the Conservative mayoral hopeful. He suggests that cutting excessive taxes and bureaucratic costs associated with new-build properties could lead to price drops of up to £100,000. This could potentially make housing more affordable for young professionals, who are increasingly being priced out of the capital.

How could house prices fall?

Sir James Cleverly claims that taxes, regulations, and other charges add approximately £100,000 to the cost of a new-build home in London. He argues that these additional costs do not contribute to the construction quality but instead inflate prices unnecessarily. By removing or reducing these expenses, he believes the price of some flats could decrease from £350,000–£400,000 to £250,000–£300,000. However, specifics on which taxes or requirements would be cut remain unclear.

Critics highlight that whilst the proposal aims to make housing more affordable, there is no guarantee that developers would pass these savings onto buyers. Ensuring that reduced costs benefit consumers directly would be a key challenge for any policy implementation.

The exodus of Londoners

Cleverly’s proposals come amidst growing concerns about the number of residents leaving London in search of more affordable housing. According to the Office for National Statistics, around 420,500 people relocated from London to other parts of the UK in the year to mid-2025, with a further 183,000 moving abroad. Whilst approximately 288,500 people moved to the capital from elsewhere in the UK, the net loss of residents remains significant.

Young professionals, in particular, are finding it increasingly difficult to make the finances work in London. Cleverly noted that destinations such as Braintree, Maidstone, Milton Keynes, and Hemel Hempstead are becoming popular choices for those seeking cheaper homes. “We are losing talent. We’re losing young people from London. That is unsustainable,” he stated.

Could the Mayor of London deliver cheaper homes?

If elected, Cleverly’s ability to implement these changes would depend on the powers available to the Mayor of London. The mayor influences housing delivery through the London Plan, which sets policies on housing targets and development. Whilst Cleverly’s proposals aim to address affordability, the feasibility of reducing house prices through these measures remains uncertain.

For homeowners and prospective buyers, these developments could have significant implications. Whilst the potential for lower house prices may be appealing, it is important to consider the broader impact on the housing market and the challenges of ensuring savings reach consumers.

item.title: Landlords face hefty bill as new rental database branded a ‘rip-off’
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Private landlords across England could face substantial new costs when the government's rental property database launches later this year. The scheme, beginning in the West Midlands from 15 December before rolling out nationally, will require all landlords to register properties at an annual fee of £65 each – potentially creating a £327m annual bill for the sector.

Industry Concerns Over Costs and Duplication

The National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) has strongly criticised the proposed charges, arguing they represent poor value for money. The £65 per property fee significantly exceeds the government's initial estimates, with the trade body warning these costs may ultimately filter through to tenants through higher rents.

Industry representatives highlight several concerns about the registration system:

  • The database duplicates information already collected through existing local authority licensing schemes, some of which cost landlords up to £2,300 per property
  • Manual upload requirements for safety certificates create unnecessary administrative burdens, particularly for portfolio landlords
  • Questions remain about whether the system will deliver sufficient benefits to justify the expense

What Landlords Need to Know

Under the Renters' Rights Act provisions, all landlords with actively let properties must complete registration by 14 November 2027. The phased rollout means landlords will have three months to register once the scheme reaches their region. Key requirements include:

  • Annual renewal of registrations at £65 per property
  • Displaying registration numbers in all property advertisements
  • Future extension to vacant properties under forthcoming legislation

Failure to comply could result in financial penalties, though exact sanction details remain unclear. The database aims to help councils identify non-compliant landlords while providing tenants with greater transparency about rental properties.

NRLA chief executive Ben Beadle commented: "A well-designed database should simplify compliance for landlords while empowering tenants. Instead we're getting a costly system that duplicates existing requirements and adds unnecessary paperwork."

The registration scheme forms part of broader changes affecting private landlords, including new ombudsman fees and increased tax on rental income from 2027. With the first phase launching imminently, landlords in the West Midlands should prepare for these new obligations in the coming months.

item.title: EYE NEWSFLASH: Greens propose sweeping rent caps as agents warn of landlord exodus
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Green Party has proposed radical reforms to the private rental sector, including strict rent caps and the abolition of leasehold tenure. The proposals, announced at their recent conference, have drawn both support from tenant groups and warnings from property industry bodies about potential unintended consequences.

Green Party's rental market proposals

Under the Green Party's plans, annual rent increases would be limited to either inflation, wage growth or 2% — whichever is lowest — for a three-year period. The policy aims to protect tenants from sudden rent hikes and prevent landlords from using excessive increases to force occupants out of properties.

Party leader Zack Polanski criticised current government policies as inadequate, arguing that stronger tenant protections are needed. The Greens' proposals go beyond Labour's rental reform plans, with additional measures including:

  • A national fair rents guarantee to maintain long-term affordability
  • The complete abolition of the leasehold system
  • Substantial increases in council housebuilding programmes

Industry concerns about rent controls

Propertymark, the professional body for estate agents, has raised significant concerns about the potential impact of rent controls. The organisation warns that such measures could accelerate the current trend of landlords leaving the market, potentially exacerbating the housing shortage.

Timothy Douglas of Propertymark highlighted the Scottish experience, where temporary rent caps reportedly led to some landlords selling properties or increasing rents between tenancies. He argued that policymakers should focus instead on increasing housing supply and encouraging responsible investment in the private rental sector.

International evidence suggests that rent controls can have several unintended consequences:

  • Reduced investment in rental properties
  • Deterioration in housing quality as maintenance budgets shrink
  • Landlords exiting the market entirely
  • Potential increase in rents between tenancies to compensate for capped increases

While tenant affordability remains a pressing issue, industry experts caution that rent controls alone cannot solve the fundamental problem of housing undersupply. Propertymark suggests that any reforms must balance immediate renter protections with long-term strategies to expand available housing stock.

As debates around rental reform continue, homeowners and landlords may wish to monitor policy developments that could affect both the rental market and broader property sector in coming years.

item.title: UK rents surge as regional divide widens
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

UK rents have climbed by nearly 5% over the past year, with tenants now paying an average of £1,581 per month compared to £1,507 in September 2022. However, the latest data highlights a growing disparity between regional rental markets, with some areas experiencing significant increases while others show signs of stagnation or decline. This trend underscores the challenges faced by renters across the country, particularly in regions where demand continues to outstrip supply.

Regional variations in rental growth

The North East has emerged as the region with the strongest rental growth, with prices soaring by 13.9% over the past year. Tenants in this area now pay an average of £1,000 per month, up from £878 in 2022. Wales followed closely behind with a 7.4% increase, bringing average rents to £994. Yorkshire and the Humber and the North West also saw notable rises, with growth rates of 6.9% and 6.1% respectively.

Meanwhile, Greater London recorded a 4.4% increase, pushing average rents to £2,306 per month. The South East experienced more modest growth at 3.1%, while the East of England became the only region to see a decline, with rents falling by 0.4% to £1,375. The East Midlands also showed signs of slowing growth, with rents increasing by just 1.8% over the year.

Monthly trends and void periods

On a monthly basis, the North East once again led the way, with rents rising by 5.6% between August and September. The North West and South West also saw increases of 3.1% and 2.5% respectively. Yorkshire and the Humber was the only region to record a slight monthly decline, although the reduction was minimal.

The average rental void period across the UK shortened slightly, dropping from 21 days in August to 20 days in September. The North East recorded the shortest voids, averaging just 11 days between tenancies, while Yorkshire and the Humber had the longest at 29 days.

Outlook for rental inflation

Despite the continued rise in rents, there are indications that the pace of rental inflation may be moderating in certain areas. William Reeve, chief executive of Goodlord, noted that while rental averages continue to outstrip inflation year-on-year, the overall rate of growth appears to be easing. This could offer some relief to tenants, though the ongoing supply and demand pressures mean rental affordability remains a concern for many.

For those navigating the rental market, staying informed about regional trends and understanding local dynamics could help in making more informed decisions. Renters might also consider exploring areas with slower growth or negotiating rental terms to manage costs effectively.

item.title: Letting agents and landlords put on alert as council steps up HMO crackdown
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Landlords and letting agents in Barnet are being urged to review their licensing obligations as the council intensifies its crackdown on unlicensed Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs). Recent enforcement efforts have seen Barnet Council conduct targeted evening inspections, with legal investigations now underway for 22 properties suspected of breaching licensing rules.

Understanding HMO Licensing Requirements

In Barnet, HMOs that meet specific criteria must hold the appropriate licence. The council maintains a public register of licensed properties, making it easier for landlords and agents to verify compliance. Beyond licensing, landlords are also required to ensure their properties meet stringent management and safety standards.

Failure to adhere to these regulations can lead to significant financial penalties. Barnet Council has already issued fines totalling £187,000 this year for HMO-related offences, with individual penalties reaching up to £40,000. This highlights the importance of ensuring properties are properly licensed and managed.

Increased Enforcement Measures

The recent evening inspections are part of a broader enforcement strategy. During the first operation, council officers visited 76 properties, identifying numerous cases of potential non-compliance. These inspections are not a one-off initiative; Barnet Council has confirmed plans to continue targeted operations across the borough over the next 12 months.

Letting and managing agents are particularly encouraged to verify the licensing status of properties under their supervision. Compliance should be reviewed regularly, especially when taking on new properties or managing existing portfolios. This proactive approach can help avoid costly penalties and legal issues.

Steps for Landlords and Agents

For landlords and agents operating in Barnet, there are several steps to ensure compliance:

  • Check whether your property requires an HMO licence using the council’s public register.
  • Ensure all licensing, management, and safety requirements are met.
  • Regularly review compliance, particularly when changes are made to the property or tenancy agreements.

By staying informed and proactive, landlords and agents can avoid the substantial penalties associated with licensing breaches.

Barnet Council’s heightened enforcement efforts underscore the importance of adhering to HMO regulations. With ongoing inspections and significant fines for non-compliance, landlords and agents are advised to act swiftly to ensure their properties meet all legal requirements.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #456
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

October has brought significant changes for UK landlords, with new right-to-rent rules taking effect alongside growing concerns about property management challenges. Recent surveys suggest landlords face mounting compliance pressures, while market data reveals rising tenant financial difficulties and longer void periods between tenancies.

Growing pressures for self-managing landlords

New research highlights the increasing difficulties facing landlords who manage properties themselves. A survey by property management firm Rushbrook found 74% of self-managing landlords report the task has become more challenging compared to three years ago. Maintenance and repairs remain the most time-consuming aspect for 52% of respondents, whilst compliance issues rank as the most stressful element.

The Renters' Reform Bill's impending changes, alongside existing regulatory requirements, have prompted many landlords to reconsider self-management. However, industry experts caution that appointing a letting agent doesn't automatically transfer legal responsibilities. Paul Endacott of 1st Avenue notes: "The biggest risk facing landlords today may be assuming someone else manages compliance when, legally, the responsibility ultimately rests with the property owner."

Tenant referencing takes on greater importance

Registry Trust data shows an 11.6% annual increase in County Court Judgments (CCJs) against consumers, with 6% of UK adults now having at least one adverse credit marker. This trend means landlords are increasingly likely to encounter prospective tenants with financial difficulties.

Allison Thompson, Chief Lettings Officer at Leaders, observes that landlords are becoming more thorough with referencing checks: "Most tenants still pass referencing processes, but with restrictions on taking rent in advance, robust referencing has become an essential tool for risk management." Industry reports indicate one in ten landlords have significantly tightened their tenant selection criteria in recent months.

Void periods lengthen as market shifts

The average void period between tenancies has extended to over three weeks across many UK regions. This extension reflects both seasonal patterns and broader market adjustments following recent legislative changes. Landlords may wish to factor these potential void periods into their financial planning, particularly when considering property investments or portfolio expansions.

For those navigating these challenges, specialist services like Landlord Law provide compliance guidance, whilst property management firms offer varying levels of support. With the rental market undergoing significant transformation, staying informed remains crucial for landlords at all experience levels.

The Renters' Reform Bill's impending changes, alongside existing regulatory requirements, have prompted many landlords to reconsider self-management. However, industry experts caution that appointing a letting agent doesn't automatically transfer legal responsibilities. Paul Endacott of 1st Avenue notes: "The biggest risk facing landlords today may be assuming someone else manages compliance when, legally, the responsibility ultimately rests with the property owner."

Tenant referencing takes on greater importance

Registry Trust data shows an 11.6% annual increase in County Court Judgments (CCJs) against consumers, with 6% of UK adults now having at least one adverse credit marker. This trend means landlords are increasingly likely to encounter prospective tenants with financial difficulties.

Industry reports indicate one in ten landlords have significantly tightened their tenant selection criteria in recent months.

The average void period between tenancies has extended to over three weeks across many UK regions. Landlords may wish to factor these potential void periods into their financial planning, particularly when considering property investments or portfolio expansions.

With the rental market undergoing significant transformation, staying informed remains crucial for landlords at all experience levels.

item.title: Letting agent fined for breaching Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A letting agent in Chesterfield has been fined over £8,600 for breaching regulations under the Renters’ Rights Act 2025. The agent issued a prohibited fixed-term tenancy agreement and instructed tenants to vacate the property after they raised concerns about its condition. Chesterfield Borough Council imposed the penalties following an investigation into the agent’s conduct, highlighting the importance of compliance with the new legislation.

Details of the Case

The case arose when tenants reported issues with their rented property shortly after moving in. Investigators found that the agent had issued a six-month fixed-term tenancy agreement, which is prohibited under the Renters’ Rights Act 2025. Additionally, the agent told the tenants to leave when they indicated they would lodge a formal complaint. The tenants subsequently moved to alternative accommodation owned by another landlord, whose identity remains undisclosed.

The council imposed two financial penalties totalling £8,652, though the agent paid a reduced amount of £7,354.20 after settling within the specified timeframe. Alongside the fines, the council issued an improvement notice requiring the property to meet housing standards. This case serves as a stark reminder to letting agents and landlords of their obligations under the new legislation.

Council’s Warning to Letting Agents

Chesterfield Borough Council has emphasised the importance of compliance with the Renters’ Rights Act. Councillor Jean Innes, the council’s cabinet member for housing, stated that the authority had engaged with local landlords and letting agents prior to the legislation’s implementation to ensure they understood the changes. She added, “We are committed to putting our communities first and making sure renters have the protection they need. This case demonstrates that we will take action where landlords and agents fail to comply with their duties.”

The council hopes this case will serve as a reminder to letting agents across Chesterfield to fully understand the recent changes to the law and their responsibilities. The Renters’ Rights Act, which came into force on 1 May 2026, aims to provide greater protection for tenants and ensure fair treatment in the rental market.

What This Means for Landlords and Agents

Landlords and letting agents may wish to review their practices to ensure compliance with the Renters’ Rights Act. Key areas to focus on include avoiding prohibited tenancy agreements and addressing tenant concerns promptly and fairly. Failure to comply could result in significant financial penalties and damage to reputation.

Tenants, on the other hand, can take reassurance from the council’s proactive approach to enforcing the legislation. Those facing issues with their rental property may consider contacting their local authority for support and guidance.

This case underscores the importance of understanding and adhering to housing legislation, benefiting both tenants and landlords in the long term.

item.title: Propertymark calls for landlord licensing schemes to be abolished
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Propertymark, a leading trade body for the property sector, has called for the abolition of discretionary landlord licensing schemes across England. The organisation argues that these local schemes, which require landlords to obtain licences to operate, impose unnecessary costs and administrative burdens. With the introduction of the national Private Rented Sector (PRS) Database, Propertymark believes there is an opportunity to streamline regulation and improve enforcement without the need for local licensing systems.

The case against local licensing schemes

In a recent position paper titled The Effectiveness of Local Authority Landlord Licensing Schemes, Propertymark questioned whether selective and additional licensing schemes provide sufficient benefits to justify their costs. The organisation highlighted that licensing fees can exceed £1,000 per property in some areas, with additional licensing schemes costing even more. For landlords managing larger portfolios, these charges can quickly escalate into tens of thousands of pounds.

Propertymark also raised concerns about the effectiveness of enforcement by local authorities. Research indicates that around two-thirds of English councils had not prosecuted a landlord in the three years leading up to the study, despite receiving an estimated 300,000 complaints annually about property conditions. Furthermore, over 84% of councils reported difficulties recruiting environmental health professionals, which could hinder their ability to enforce housing standards effectively.

Proposals for reform

Propertymark has proposed several reforms to improve the current system. The trade body advocates for greater transparency regarding how councils spend licensing income, suggesting that fees should be directly linked to inspections and enforcement efforts. Additionally, it has called for a national cap on administration costs, limiting them to 20% of licensing fees.

Tim Thomas, Propertymark’s Senior Policy and Campaigns Officer, emphasised the need for clarity and enforcement. “Landlords should be able to see a clear connection between the fees they pay and the improvements being delivered in their local housing market,” he said. “The priority must be enforcement. A licensing system should not become an end in itself, particularly where councils already have extensive powers to identify and act against unsafe or poorly managed housing.”

The national PRS database

The introduction of the national PRS Database, known as the Register Your Rental Property service, is seen as a potential replacement for local licensing schemes. The first phase of the database is scheduled to launch on 15 December 2026, beginning in the West Midlands before rolling out across England over the following 12 months. Once fully operational, the database will require all landlords actively letting properties in England to register their details.

Propertymark believes the national database could simplify regulation, reduce costs for landlords, and improve enforcement by providing a centralised system for monitoring compliance. This shift could mark a significant step towards a more efficient and transparent private rental sector.

As the property sector awaits the implementation of the PRS Database, Propertymark’s proposals have sparked debate about the future of landlord licensing and the best ways to ensure safe and well-managed rental properties across England.

item.title: House prices hit decade-high affordability – but buyers face a sting in the tail
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New data suggests UK housing affordability has reached its most favourable level in nearly a decade, though rising mortgage rates mean many buyers continue to face financial pressures. According to recent analysis, the average property now costs 7.3 times annual earnings, down from 7.6 times last year – marking the lowest house price-to-income ratio since 2015.

Wage growth outpaces property prices

The improved affordability ratio stems from a widening gap between earnings and house price growth. Over the past year, average salaries increased by 4.5% to £40,790, while property values rose just 0.5% to £299,131. First-time buyers have seen some relief too, with their price-to-earnings ratio falling from 6.1 to 5.9 as prices crept up by only 0.3%.

However, these headline figures don't tell the full story. Despite improved affordability ratios, homeowners now face higher monthly repayments due to elevated mortgage rates. The average monthly mortgage payment has increased by £57 over the past year, reaching £1,157.

Regional variations in affordability

The most significant improvements occurred in England's priciest housing markets. The South East saw its ratio drop from 9.7 to 9.1, while London's fell from 10.9 to 10.3. Eastern England and the South West also recorded notable declines to 8.2 and 7.7 respectively. Nevertheless, London and the South East remain the nation's least affordable regions.

Other areas showed more modest changes:

  • North East: 5.1 to 5.0
  • Scotland: Remained steady at 5.3
  • North West: 6.5 to 6.3
  • Yorkshire and the Humber: 6.0 to 5.8

Northern Ireland proved the exception, with house prices rising 7.4% – nearly double the 3.7% wage growth – pushing its ratio up from 5.8 to 6.0.

Ongoing challenges for buyers

While the figures suggest some positive movement, industry experts caution that affordability pressures persist. Mortgage rates remain substantially higher than recent historic lows, and saving for deposits continues to challenge first-time buyers in particular.

Some borrowers might consider exploring mortgage products designed for those with smaller deposits, though these won't suit every situation. As always, prospective buyers may wish to seek independent financial advice to understand their full range of options in the current market.

For those considering a property purchase, weighing both house price affordability and ongoing mortgage costs remains crucial when assessing what's financially manageable in the long term.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Key leadership changes are underway in the UK property sector, with notable appointments and transitions shaping the future of several prominent estate agency brands. These developments highlight the evolving strategies of major players in the market, particularly in response to regulatory changes and regional growth ambitions.

New Leadership at Lomond’s Southern Region

Lomond has announced the appointment of Neil McGimpsey as chief revenue officer for its southern region. McGimpsey, who previously served as Lomond’s chief operating officer, will now oversee the performance and growth of the group’s southern agency brands, including Charters, Miles & Barr, Prospect, and Ocean. His extensive experience in the property sector, including 15 years in senior roles at Foxtons and a stint as chief executive of Druce & Co, positions him as a strong candidate to drive Lomond’s regional strategy forward.

McGimpsey’s appointment follows the departure of Rob Mott, founder of Charters, who is stepping down after 18 years. During his tenure, Mott played a pivotal role in expanding Charters and establishing it as a leading brand within Lomond’s portfolio. Lomond’s chief executive, Paul Geddes, praised Mott’s contributions and expressed confidence in McGimpsey’s ability to lead the southern region into its next phase of growth.

Expansion and Regional Focus

Lomond’s decision to appoint McGimpsey aligns with its broader strategy to strengthen its regional management structure. The group now operates 14 estate and letting agency brands across England and Scotland, reflecting its commitment to maintaining a strong presence in key markets. McGimpsey’s leadership will be instrumental in navigating challenges posed by recent regulatory changes, such as those introduced by the Renters’ Rights Act, while capitalising on emerging opportunities in the southern region.

In a statement, McGimpsey expressed his enthusiasm for the role, acknowledging the legacy left by Mott and the potential for further success. He emphasised the importance of collaboration across Lomond’s teams to build on the achievements already made in the southern region.

Savills Strengthens Salisbury Team

Meanwhile, Savills has bolstered its Salisbury residential team with the appointment of Camilla Elwell as director. With nearly 14 years of experience in the property industry, Elwell brings a wealth of knowledge to the role. She began her career at Savills in 2012 as a negotiator and later joined the firm’s Country House Department, where she honed her expertise in high-value properties.

Elwell’s promotion underscores Savills’ commitment to nurturing talent within its ranks and enhancing its regional capabilities. Her appointment is expected to strengthen the firm’s presence in Salisbury and contribute to its reputation for delivering exceptional service in the residential property market.

These leadership changes reflect the dynamic nature of the UK property sector, with major players like Lomond and Savills adapting to market demands and regulatory shifts. Homeowners and property professionals alike may wish to keep an eye on these developments, as they could influence trends and opportunities in the housing market.
